## The ticket

Six months later. Lakeshore's scheduled document-control audit — the one your Quality Analyst
built specifically to be the Owen Pruitt CAPA's (corrective and preventive action)
effectiveness check — is running across every collection site this week. She walks into your
office with the site-by-site findings, and for once she's not holding a problem.

"Every site: current downtime SOP (standard operating procedure) physically in the binder, dated
acknowledgment of receipt on file from the site lead, deferred-donor list refresh cadence matches
the current revision. Zero exceptions. Brookfield included."

Then she puts a second, smaller item on your desk. Two weeks ago, Lakeshore revised the same
downtime SOP again — a minor clarification, nothing safety-critical. The new tracked-distribution
process caught something on its own, without anyone chasing it down: one satellite site's lead
had left the organization, and the acknowledgment never came back. The system flagged it as
overdue after 72 hours. Quality followed up, found an interim lead hadn't been told they now owned
that binder, fixed it, and got a signed acknowledgment before the new revision's effective date.

"That's the tracked-distribution process actually working," she says. "Not a document existing
somewhere. A document *landing*, and someone checking that it did."

You sit with that for a second, because it's the cleanest possible closing argument for
everything this whole story has been about. Six months ago, a superseded procedure sat in a
binder at a satellite site because nothing verified it had ever been replaced. Today, a *different*
kind of gap — a departed site lead — tried to create the exact same failure mode, and a control
built specifically to catch it did. Same shape of risk. Different outcome, because the control
this course has been building toward finally exists.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

This module lives in **QSE 6** of AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework —
**Documents and Records** — the drawer module 1 told you holds the document lifecycle and record
retention. Everything else in this course's through-line story has been building toward this
drawer without naming it: the SOP that failed at Brookfield, the acknowledgment module 4 just
built, the binder itself. This module gives that machinery its name and its rules.

Start with the failure mode this QSE exists to prevent, because it's the one this whole story
already showed you in full: **a document can be perfectly correct, approved, and current — and
still fail completely — if the wrong version is what's physically present where the work actually
happens.** Brookfield's binder wasn't missing a procedure. It had one. It was the *wrong* one, and
nothing in Lakeshore's process, as it existed six months ago, would have caught that until
something went wrong downstream. Document control exists to make "the current version is the
only version anyone can actually use" true in practice, not just true in theory.

You already run something structurally identical: **knowledge management**, the ITIL practice of
keeping the information your teams rely on accurate, current, and findable. You've lived the
failure mode too — a knowledge-base article that's technically still in the system, still
findable by search, but describes a process three versions out of date, and someone follows it
anyway because nothing told them not to. That's Brookfield's binder in IT clothing. The bridge
holds all the way through, with one addition the quality world insists on that a knowledge base
usually doesn't: **findable isn't good enough. The current version has to be the *only* version
physically present at the point of use, and every superseded version has to be actively removed
or unmistakably marked obsolete — not just outranked by a newer one sitting in a central system
somewhere.** "It's on SharePoint, so everyone has the latest" is exactly the same shape of false
confidence as "the current SOP revision is filed centrally, so Brookfield has it" — six months
ago, it didn't. A knowledge base with version history is a good start. Document control demands
proof the old version is actually gone from where people work, not just superseded on paper.

One more bridge, in one paragraph: document control is also **configuration management**. A
controlled document is a versioned configuration item (CI) with a defined baseline (the approved,
effective revision). The master document list Quality maintains is functionally Lakeshore's CMDB
(configuration management database) for procedures. But a CMDB that's accurate centrally while a
stale configuration is still deployed in production isn't in control of anything — the same gap
tracked distribution and acknowledgment now closes for Lakeshore's satellite-site binders.

## Document control in plain English

Start with the distinction this whole module rests on, because the Owen Pruitt story is the
clearest possible way to teach it: **a document tells you what to do. A record proves what you
actually did.**

- A **document** — an SOP, a policy, a work instruction, a form template before it's filled in —
  is instructional. It exists before the work happens and guides it. Brookfield's downtime SOP,
  whichever revision was in the binder, is a document.
- A **record** is evidentiary. It's created *by* doing the work, and it proves the work happened,
  when, and by whom. A completed downtime paper transaction log, a signed temperature chart, and
  — the one this course built directly — **the site lead's signed, dated acknowledgment that the
  current SOP revision actually arrived and was put in the binder** are all records. That
  acknowledgment isn't a nice-to-have paperwork step. It's the specific piece of evidence that
  proves the document reached the point of use, as opposed to merely having been sent.

Notice the sentence you'd actually say to an assessor: *the document is the current downtime SOP;
the record is the acknowledgment proving Brookfield's copy of it is the current one.* Two
different objects, two different jobs, and confusing them is exactly the trap below.

Now the lifecycle every controlled document moves through, in order, and each stage has to leave
its own evidence:

**1. Draft.** Someone writes or revises the procedure. No controlling authority yet — it's not
usable for real work.

**2. Review and approval.** Someone with the authority to approve — for a downtime SOP, that's
Quality, the same function that approved the change-control record in the last module — reviews
the content and signs off, with a dated signature. This is the same approval discipline
`change-control-for-regulated-systems` already walked you through for the *change*; document
control is where that approval turns into the document's own formal record.

**3. Issue, with an effective date.** The approved document becomes controlled: it gets a version
number, an effective date, and gets distributed to every location where the work it governs
actually happens. This is where module 4's fix lives — the tracked distribution list with
required signed, dated acknowledgment of receipt from every site lead. Issue isn't complete when
the document is sent. It's complete when every site that needs it has confirmed, in writing, that
they have it.

**4. Periodic review.** On a defined interval, someone re-reads the document to confirm it's still
accurate and still reflects how the work is actually done — not waiting for something to break
before checking.

**5. Revision.** When something changes — a regulatory update, a process improvement, a CAPA's
fix — the document goes back to draft, gets re-approved, and gets re-issued as a new version, with
a new effective date. This is exactly what happened two weeks ago with the downtime SOP's minor
clarification.

**6. Retirement and obsolescence.** The superseded version stops being valid. This is the stage
that actually failed six months ago, and it's the one this module spends the most time on below,
because "retired" has to mean something concrete, not just "a newer version now exists somewhere."

One more piece worth naming, briefly: **controlled versus uncontrolled copies.** A controlled copy
is tracked — Quality knows exactly where it is and can guarantee it gets updated. An uncontrolled
copy (a printout someone made for convenience, a PDF saved to a personal drive) isn't tracked, and
nobody can guarantee it ever gets the next revision. Brookfield's binder was *supposed* to be a
controlled copy; the gap module 3 found was that Lakeshore's process couldn't actually prove it
was being controlled — controlled in name, uncontrolled in practice. The same logic covers
**external documents** — a vendor's equipment manual, the AABB Standards themselves — which also
need a current-version control, in one sentence, not built out further here.

Last thing, in one sentence, because it matters and this module doesn't own it: Friday night's
paper downtime transactions, once filled in, are records — later transcribed into BECS (Blood
Establishment Computer Software) during Monday's reconciliation, which is exactly the hybrid
paper-to-electronic handoff that caught Owen Pruitt's deferral in the first place. A later course,
`data-integrity-and-records`, covers what makes that transcription itself trustworthy (ALCOA+,
audit trails, Part 11) — this module just needed you to see where the paper record's story
continues.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(b), "must be available…" sentence | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b" | Written procedures "must be available to the personnel for use in the areas where the procedures are performed." | Already the regulatory floor in the last two modules. Here it's the exact clause the tracked-distribution-and-acknowledgment process exists to satisfy — proof the current revision is physically present where the work happens, not just approved somewhere centrally. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(a)(1) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph a, sub-one" | Records must be maintained *concurrently* with the work, legible, indelible, identifying who did the work, dated, and complete enough to trace every step. | The baseline for **Good Documentation Practices**: this is why a signed, dated acknowledgment — not a verbal "yes, we got it" — is the record that actually satisfies document control. |
| 21 CFR 606.120(b)(2) | "Six-oh-six point one-twenty, paragraph b, sub-two" | Obsolete labels must be *destroyed* — not just outranked by a current label existing somewhere. | Part 606's own closest analog to this module's central point, just applied to container labels instead of procedures. Worth reading carefully — see below. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(d) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph d" | Sets the retention clock for individual product records — at least 10 years after processing is completed, or 6 months past the product's latest expiration date, whichever is later. Already taught in `reading-a-cfr-citation`. | Referenced here only as a pointer: document and record retention schedules can run on different clocks than this donor/product-record retention rule, and Lakeshore's document-control SOP has to say which schedule governs which kind of record. Not re-derived here. |

## The actual text

606.100(b)'s availability clause, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md` — the same
sentence the last two modules already built toward, worth its own full weight here because this
module is where it finally gets satisfied end to end:

> Such procedures must be available to the personnel for use in the areas where the procedures
> are performed.

Read "available" and "for use" as doing real work, together. A document existing in a binder
somewhere isn't "available for use" if it's the wrong revision — availability means the *current*
procedure is what's actually there.

606.160(a)(1)'s Good Documentation Practice standard, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> Records shall be maintained concurrently with the performance of each significant step in the
> collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of each unit of blood
> and blood components so that all steps can be clearly traced. All records shall be legible and
> indelible, and shall identify the person performing the work, include dates of the various
> entries, show test results as well as the interpretation of the results, show the expiration
> date assigned to specific products, and be as detailed as necessary to provide a complete
> history of the work performed.

That's written for product records, but the discipline it demands — concurrent, legible,
attributable, dated, complete — is exactly what a real document-control record has to be too. A
site lead's acknowledgment scrawled from memory two weeks after the fact, undated, isn't a record
in this sense. Signed and dated at the moment the document actually arrived is.

Now the genuinely interesting one, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.120.md`, a section not
quoted by any earlier lesson in this curriculum:

> Each type of label representing different products shall be stored and maintained in a manner
> to prevent mixups, and stocks of obsolete labels shall be destroyed.

Sit with that sentence next to this whole module's central point. Part 606 *does* require obsolete
material to be physically removed — for container labels. It doesn't say "keep a current version
on file and trust staff to reach for the right one." It says **destroy the obsolete stock.** That's
the same instinct this module teaches for documents: an obsolete version has to stop being
physically available, not just stop being the authoritative one. Part 606 simply never extends
that instinct from labels to procedures. Here's the tiering worth stating plainly, the same way
modules 3 and 4 already did for CAPA and change control: **the phrase "document control" does not
appear anywhere in 21 CFR Part 606, and nothing in Part 606's text requires a periodic review
interval or a formal obsolete-document-removal process for SOPs.** The regulatory floor is
606.100(b): procedures must exist, be maintained, and be available where used. The *mechanics*
that get you there reliably — draft, approval, effective dates, periodic review, controlled
distribution with acknowledgment, retirement — are AABB's Quality Systems Framework, under the
Documents and Records QSE, binding on Lakeshore through accreditation, not through Part 606's own
words.

Retention, in one line and not re-derived: 606.160(d), already fully taught in
`reading-a-cfr-citation`, sets the clock for *individual product records* — at least 10 years
past processing, or 6 months past the product's latest expiration date, whichever is later. A
document-control SOP itself, and records like distribution acknowledgments, can sit on a
different retention schedule than that product-record clock; Lakeshore's document-control
procedure has to say what that schedule is for each record type, a level of detail this module
doesn't build out further.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor reviewing Lakeshore's document control wouldn't stop at "does a current version of
this SOP exist." They'd ask for proof of exactly the thing that failed at Brookfield and exactly
the thing that just worked two weeks ago.

**Positive evidence that obsolete versions were physically removed or clearly marked obsolete —
at the point of use, site by site.** Not "the master list shows revision 4 is current." A dated
record, from each site, that the *old* copy is gone and the new one is in its place. This is
precisely what the six-month audit your QA just ran produced, and precisely what didn't exist six
months before that.

**Document versus record, correctly distinguished in the quality manual.** An assessor who asks
"what's your document, and what's your record proving it was followed" and gets a blank look, or
gets the same object named as both, has found a real gap — not a technicality. Lakeshore's answer
now: the downtime SOP is the document; the site lead's signed, dated acknowledgment is the record.

**Retention schedules actually being followed**, for both documents (how long superseded
revisions are archived before permanent disposal, and in what form) and records (how long
acknowledgments, training records, and audit findings themselves are kept) — checked against
whatever Lakeshore's own document-control SOP specifies those intervals to be, not assumed to
match the 606.160(d) product-record clock by default.

**A functioning distribution mechanism with a real failure-detection path** — exactly the thing
the departed-site-lead catch just demonstrated. An assessor doesn't just want to see that
distribution happened; they want to see what happens when it *doesn't*, on schedule, the first
time.

## Common traps

**"The current version exists in our system, so we're in control."** This is Brookfield's exact
failure, restated as a policy. A master document list with the correct current revision proves
Quality knows what the current version *should* be everywhere. It proves nothing about what's
actually sitting in a binder at a site nobody's checked recently. Document control isn't
satisfied by a correct central record — it's satisfied by proof that the correct version, and
only the correct version, is what a person reaches for at the point of use.

**Confusing a document with a record.** Calling the downtime SOP itself "the record" — or treating
a blank, unsigned acknowledgment form as if having the form on file were the same as having proof
someone signed it — collapses two different pieces of evidence into one. An assessor asking "show
me the record that proves this document reached the site" wants the signed acknowledgment, not
another copy of the SOP.

**Treating a training record as ongoing proof of compliance.** A training sign-off from eighteen
months ago proves a person once learned a procedure that existed at that time. It doesn't prove
they're following the *current* revision today, and it definitely doesn't prove the current
revision is what's physically in front of them. This is a genuinely common substitution — "they
were trained on it" standing in for "they have it and are using it" — and it's the same trap as
mistaking implementation evidence for verification evidence, which `change-control-for-regulated-
systems` already flagged for a different step of this same story.

## What this means for your job

- **When your QA reports a document as "current," ask what proves the old version is physically
  gone from every site that had it** — not what proves the new version exists somewhere central.
  "Current" and "controlled" aren't the same claim.
- **Ask for the document and the record as two separate artifacts, every time.** If a review
  produces only one object doing both jobs, something's missing — usually the record proving the
  document actually landed.
- **Watch for a distribution mechanism that has no failure path.** A process that assumes every
  site lead will respond, with nothing flagging the one who doesn't, is the same unverified "mail
  it and hope" gap module 4 already caught once. The departed-site-lead catch worked because the
  system flagged silence as a problem, not because everyone happened to respond.
- **Don't accept a training record as proof of current compliance.** Ask what confirms the person
  has, and is using, today's revision — not what confirms they once sat through a session.
- **Push for periodic review dates on your own calendar, not just Quality's.** A document that's
  never revisited until something breaks is running on the same "we'll notice if it's wrong"
  assumption that let Brookfield's binder go unchecked for who knows how long before Owen Pruitt's
  donation surfaced it.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "21 CFR Part 606 requires us to remove obsolete SOP revisions from active use and destroy them." True or false?

False, as worded — and worth getting right, because the honest answer is more interesting than a
flat yes. Part 606 never uses the phrase "document control," names no periodic-review interval,
and sets no obsolete-document-removal requirement for procedures. It *does* require obsolete
container labels to be destroyed (606.120(b)(2)) — the same underlying instinct this module
teaches, just scoped to labels, not SOPs. The regulatory floor for procedures is narrower:
606.100(b) requires that written procedures be established, maintained, and available where
performed — which an obsolete version sitting in an active binder plainly violates in effect, but
the text never spells out "remove and destroy" as the mechanism. That structured lifecycle —
issue, periodic review, retirement, controlled removal — is AABB's Quality Systems Framework,
under the Documents and Records QSE. Tell your CIO: the law requires the right procedure to
actually be there; AABB's Standards supply the disciplined process that proves the wrong one
isn't.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A site lead's training record shows they completed downtime-procedure training eight months ago. Does that prove Brookfield is currently compliant?

No. A training record proves a point-in-time event: this person sat through training on whatever
revision existed eight months ago. It says nothing about whether the SOP has since been revised,
whether the current revision actually reached the site, or whether anyone confirmed it's what's
physically in the binder today. That's precisely the substitution this module's traps section
warns against — training completion standing in for document currency. The record that actually
proves current compliance is the signed, dated acknowledgment tied to the *current* revision's
distribution, not a training record from any point before it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Six months ago, Brookfield's superseded downtime SOP caused a reportable deviation. Today, the six-month document-control audit found zero sites out of compliance, and a separate distribution miss (the departed site lead) was caught and corrected before its effective date. Is the CAPA from `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness` now closed?

Yes — this is the effectiveness check that module 3 wrote before anyone knew how it would turn
out, and it passed clean against the exact pre-agreed criterion: zero sites holding a superseded
revision or a stale deferred-donor list at the scheduled audit. The departed-site-lead catch is
worth noticing separately, though — it's not part of the CAPA's own effectiveness criterion, but
it's strong independent evidence that the underlying mechanism (not just the specific binder swap)
is doing its job: it caught a *different* failure mode with the same shape, before it became a
new deviation. That's what closing a CAPA on real data, rather than on "we implemented the fix,"
is supposed to feel like.
:::

## Where this goes next

Here's what actually changed at Lakeshore because of one Friday night at Brookfield: a
document-control process that used to run on an honor system — send the new revision, assume it
arrived — now runs on tracked distribution with required, dated acknowledgment, verified at
issuance and re-checked on a standing audit schedule. The CAPA that gap produced is closed, on
real effectiveness data, not on the say-so that the fix had shipped. That's modules 2 through 5,
one event, start to finish: discovery and reportability, root cause and a provable fix, a formally
controlled change, and a document-control system that now actually keeps the wrong version out of
the building.

Every one of those four modules made risk calls along the way — how severe an extent-of-condition
gap was, how likely a distribution miss might be, how much scrutiny a given change deserved — using
the likelihood/severity/detectability vocabulary you already had going in. None of that was run
through a formal, documented risk process; it was reasoned through informally, the way most real
decisions actually get made. `quality-risk-management`, the next module, steps back and gives that
informal reasoning a real structure: ICH Q9(R1)'s risk-management process, applied to a decision
this course's own story has already been quietly making all along.
